title: Framework 4.8: the end of the road
sub: Why it stopped evolving and why you still need it
cards/0/body:
.NET Framework is installed once per system and shared by everyone. Version 4.x replaces the previous 4.x in place: install 4.8, and every app built for 4.5 now runs on 4.8.

So any change in behavior risks breaking thousands of other people's apps. Serious changes became almost impossible.
cards/1/q: Why is Framework so hard to evolve?
cards/1/options/0: One shared copy for the whole system: a change can break every installed app
cards/1/explain: Modern .NET versions install side by side, and each app picks its own.
cards/2/body:
.NET Framework 4.8 shipped in 2019, and 4.8.1 added ARM64 support in 2022. No new features are coming, only security fixes.

It is supported for as long as the Windows version it ships with. So "legacy" does not mean "dead".
cards/3/task: Find the year .NET Framework 4.8 came out. What else shipped that year?
cards/4/title: Why you still need it: plugins
cards/4/body:
A plugin is a DLL that a host app loads into its own process. That means the plugin runs on whatever runtime the host runs on.

Revit 2024 and AutoCAD 2024 run on .NET Framework 4.8, so their plugins must target Framework 4.8 too. Revit and AutoCAD 2025 moved to .NET 8.
cards/5/q: A Revit 2024 plugin is built for net8.0. What happens?
cards/5/options/0: Revit will not load it: Revit 2024 runs on .NET Framework 4.8
cards/5/explain: The host decides the runtime. The plugin adapts to the host, not the other way around.
cards/6/q: What is true about .NET Framework 4.8? Select all that apply.
cards/6/options/2: It will get new C# versions and new APIs
cards/6/options/3: Plugins for older Revit and AutoCAD need it
cards/6/explain: Officially, Framework supports C# up to 7.3. Many newer language features still compile for it, but it will never get new APIs.
cards/7/explain: net48 is how a project names .NET Framework 4.8.
